title: Area of Triangles and Parallelograms Grade 6 (Skill Practice) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms Grade 6 + Quiz
meta_desc: Master area of triangles and parallelograms grade 6: base × height, the 1/2 rule, spotting the true height, plus a free 8-question quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: The single mistake I see most in Grade 6 is multiplying by the slant side instead of the perpendicular height. Here is how to get area of triangles and parallelograms right every time, with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 6 student a parallelogram with the base marked 10 cm, the slant side marked 8 cm, and the perpendicular height marked 6 cm, and watch what happens. More often than not they reach for the 8, because it looks like the side you are ‘supposed’ to use. That one habit — grabbing the slant side instead of the height — is the reason so many marks vanish. Getting the area of triangles and parallelograms grade 6 right is less about the formula and more about picking the correct measurement to plug in.

The good news is that two clean formulas cover the whole topic, and once a child can spot the perpendicular height on a diagram, the rest is just careful arithmetic. Let me walk through exactly what I teach, in order.

The two formulas you actually need

Everything in this chapter rests on two rules, and they are related:

  • Area of a parallelogram = base × height
  • Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height

Notice the triangle is exactly half the parallelogram. That is not a coincidence — any triangle is half of a parallelogram built on the same base and the same height. I get students to draw a parallelogram, slice it along the diagonal, and see the two identical triangles fall out. Once they have seen it, the ½ stops feeling like a rule they have to memorise and starts feeling obvious.

What ‘base’ and ‘height’ really mean

The base is any one side you choose. The height is the perpendicular distance from that base to the opposite corner (for a triangle) or the opposite side (for a parallelogram). Perpendicular means it meets the base at a right angle — the little square symbol in the diagram. The height is almost never the slanted side you can see; it is the straight-up distance, and it is usually drawn as a dashed line inside the shape.

The slant-side trap (read this twice)

Here is the mistake that costs the most marks. In a parallelogram, the two slanted sides are longer than the height. The exam deliberately gives you the slant length to tempt you. For area you must ignore it and use the perpendicular height.

Take that first example: base 10 cm, slant side 8 cm, height 6 cm. The area is 10 × 6 = 60 cm², not 10 × 8 = 80 cm². When is the slant side useful? For perimeter, never for area. I tell my students: if the question says ‘area’, put a line through the slant number before you start.

Worked examples, step by step

ShapeGivenFormulaWorkingArea
Parallelogrambase 12 cm, height 5 cmbase × height12 × 560 cm²
Trianglebase 8 cm, height 7 cm½ × base × height½ × 8 × 728 cm²
Parallelogrambase 9 cm, height 6 cmbase × height9 × 654 cm²
Trianglebase 10 cm, height 9 cm½ × base × height½ × 10 × 945 cm²

A small ordering tip for the triangle: halve the even number first. For ½ × 8 × 7, do ½ × 8 = 4, then 4 × 7 = 28. It keeps the numbers whole and cuts silly errors.

Working backwards: finding a missing base or height

The harder questions flip it around. You are told the area and one measurement, and asked for the other. This is where most of the real thinking lives, and it is worth practising until it is automatic.

Parallelogram: area given

Suppose a parallelogram has area 72 cm² and base 8 cm. Since area = base × height, you divide: height = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 cm. Simple, once you trust the rearranging.

Triangle: watch the half

A triangle has area 30 cm² and base 12 cm — find the height. The catch is the ½. Because area = ½ × base × height, first multiply the area by 2 to undo the half: 30 × 2 = 60. Then divide by the base: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm. Forgetting to double the area first is the second most common error in this chapter, right after the slant-side trap.

  • Parallelogram: missing height = area ÷ base (or missing base = area ÷ height)
  • Triangle: missing height = (2 × area) ÷ base (or missing base = (2 × area) ÷ height)

A quick routine that stops errors

Before touching a calculator, I make students run a three-second checklist. Is it a triangle or a parallelogram? That decides whether the ½ is in play. Which number is the perpendicular height, and which is the slant side I should ignore? Are the units the same — you cannot mix cm and m — and is my answer in square units? Nine times out of ten, a wrong answer in this topic fails one of those three checks, not the multiplication.

One honest caveat: diagrams are not always drawn to scale, and the height is sometimes shown outside the shape for an obtuse triangle. Do not panic when that happens — the rule is unchanged. You still use the perpendicular distance to the base, even if the dashed line sits beyond the triangle’s edge.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz built on exactly these skills — base × height, the ½ rule, spotting the real height, and finding a missing measurement. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they slip on. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end has plenty of questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Area of Triangles and Parallelograms Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on base × height, the half rule, finding the true height, and working backwards from a given area. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 area of triangles and parallelograms

questions.q: A parallelogram has base 12 cm and height 5 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 12 × 5 = 60 cm².

questions.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and height 7 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 8 × 7 = 28 cm².

questions.q: A parallelogram has base 10 cm, slant side 8 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Use the perpendicular height, not the slant side: 10 × 6 = 60 cm². The 8 cm is a distractor.

questions.q: Which measurement do you use for the area of a parallelogram?
questions.explanation: Area needs the perpendicular height — the straight distance between the two bases, meeting them at a right angle.

questions.q: A parallelogram has area 72 cm² and base 8 cm. What is its height?
questions.explanation: Rearrange base × height = area, so height = area ÷ base = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 cm.

questions.q: A triangle has area 30 cm² and base 12 cm. What is its height?
questions.explanation: Double the area to undo the half: 30 × 2 = 60, then 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm.

questions.q: How does the area of a triangle relate to a parallelogram on the same base and height?
questions.explanation: A parallelogram splits along its diagonal into two identical triangles, so each triangle is half the parallelogram — that is where the 1/2 comes from.

questions.q: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 9 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: 1/2 × 10 × 9: halve the 10 first to get 5, then 5 × 9 = 45 cm².

faq.q: Why is the area of a triangle half of base times height?
faq.a: Any triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram built on the same base and the same height. Draw a parallelogram, cut along its diagonal, and you get two identical triangles — so one triangle is half the parallelogram, which is why we multiply by ½.

faq.q: How do I know which measurement is the height and which is the slant side?
faq.a: The height is the perpendicular distance to the base — it meets the base at a right angle and is usually shown as a dashed line with a small square symbol. The slant side is the tilted edge you can see. For area, always use the perpendicular height, never the slant side.

faq.q: Do the units for area change from centimetres?
faq.a: Yes. Length is measured in cm or m, but area is always in square units — cm² or m². If your final answer for an area does not carry a small 2, something has gone wrong.

faq.q: How do I find a missing base or height when the area is given?
faq.a: For a parallelogram, divide: height = area ÷ base. For a triangle, double the area first to cancel the ½, then divide: height = (2 × area) ÷ base. Forgetting to double the area is the most common slip.
